vignette.name: Writing Max Objects in Python
vignette.p: PythonTap runs a Python class as a Max object. You write the class in a file; the object loads it, makes Max attributes of its fields and Max messages of its methods, and loads it again every time you save the file. There are two objects:

ul.li: tap.python~ runs the class as an audio object: its process() method runs on the signal.
tap.python runs it as an ordinary object, without audio: what a method returns is what the object outputs.

vignette.p: Both come with CPython 3.13, numpy and attrs, and share one interpreter: Python's own modules, anything you install into the package's runtime, and your own helper modules are there for every class. This guide is the short form; the PythonTap book, online, says every rule in full, and the tutorials build three objects step by step.

Classes live in the package's python folder. [tap.python~ name] or [tap.python name] loads python/name.py and instantiates the class name in it: the file, the class and the argument share one name, which must be a valid Python identifier. Without an argument, python/default.py is loaded. Open the file in any text editor; other files in the folder can be imported by the class as helper modules.
vignette.h2: Fields are attributes, methods are messages

ul.li: Attributes. Each public field with a type annotation is a Max attribute: an int a long, a float a float64, a bool an on/off toggle, anything else a symbol. Set it in the object box (gain 0.5), by message (gain 0.5), with attrui or getattr.

Messages. Each public method is a message, called according to its signature: its type hints convert the message's arguments, parameters with defaults are optional, and *args takes any number. Methods named int, float, symbol, bang and list answer those standard messages, and a last parameter hinted list[float] or np.ndarray takes all the arguments left, as one list or array.

Names Max keeps. A few names belong to Max or the object (dsp64, assist, notify, filechanged, ...): a method or field of such a name is not exposed, and the console says so, so that you can rename it.

vignette.p: A method named process runs on the signal, in one of two forms chosen by its type hints: process(self, x: float) -> float is called once per sample — simplest to write, but every line of Python in it runs tens of thousands of times a second — and process(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray once per signal vector, where numpy works on the whole vector at C speed: the form for anything with real work in it. Its parameters are the object's signal inlets and its return hint its outlets (tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] for two), and an optional prepare(self, sample_rate: float, vector_size: int) is told Max's audio settings before the audio starts and whenever they change. Wrap the object in mc. to run one instance per channel.

By default process() runs on the audio thread, so anything else holding Python's interpreter — a reload, a message, another instance — holds the audio up meanwhile. With mode worker it runs on a thread of its own, latency milliseconds behind the audio, and the audio thread never waits for Python.

tap.python outputs what a method returns, before the message returns: nothing for None, a number for a number, symbol and the string for a str, a list for a list or a numpy array — or the message a list names, when its first element is a str — and, from a method hinted -> tuple[str, int], one value per outlet, right to left. The object has as many outlets as its widest such hint, and a dumpout at the right that answers get followed by an attribute's name. A method named anything answers every message the class has no method for, with the message's name first.

A message runs on the thread it arrives on, as any Max object's does: Max's main thread, or the scheduler thread with Overdrive on — where a long method holds the scheduler for its duration. With Scheduler in Audio Interrupt on, that is the audio thread, and the object says so once: send such messages through deferlow to run them on the main thread instead.

Save the file and the object loads it again, in place: the attributes and messages follow the new class, attribute values carry over, and audio continues with the new code without a gap. A save that changes process()'s inputs or outputs, or a tap.python class's outlets, changes the object's inlets and outlets to match, keeping the patch cords of those that stay. Every object using the file shares one execution of it per save, and the console says so once. Send filechanged to reload by hand.

print() writes to the Max console. An exception your code raises — in a method, an attribute's validator, the constructor, or the file itself — prints its traceback there and never takes Max down; sys.exit() included. A file that fails to load is reported once, and the object outputs silence, or nothing, until a save fixes it. What no object can catch is what happens below Python: a crash in a C extension, os._exit(), or a loop that never ends.
